newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. warns against Mideast winners and losers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns against Mideast winners and losers.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher sought to relaunch Israeli-Palestinian peace talks by warning that accord was impossible if one side won and the other side lost.

He disputed any assessment that a two-day crisis summit in Washington last week was a success for hardline Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a disappointment, if not an outright failure, for Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Christopher, on a follow-up visit to Israel, said the media had misread the summit's results and U.S. officials stressed that any agreement must meet both Israeli and Palestinian requirements.

Any perception of Israel gaining more under a U.S.-led peace process would further undermine already difficult negotiations, which resumed on Sunday night at Erez on the Israel-Gaza border, as well as U.S. credibility in the Arab world generally.

Christopher carried -- at least publicly -- similar messages to both sides. "Agreements simply will not be possible if there are winners and losers," he said after talks with Netanyahu in Jerusalem. "Both sides need to be able to win."

Washington launched its effort to get negotiations going again after the most serious Israeli-Palestinian clashes since the 1993 Oslo accords gave self-rule to Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The two sides are focusing first on implementing remaining aspects of the deal, especially the long-delayed redeployment of Israeli troops in the West Bank town of Hebron.

Christopher, who has spent more time on the Middle East than any other issue, urged them to take more care with their public statements and not to reveal bargaining proposals in advance of sharing them with the other side.

He pressed them to understand better the needs of the other side and to take this into account when considering a peace deal. He also stressed a need for quick significant results so that even more devastating violence did not erupt.
Netanyahu and Arafat -- at U.S. urging -- recommitted themselves on Sunday to fulfilling the 1993 Oslo accords. But this affirmation, considered so critical, quickly became embroiled in controversy.

Israel has delayed carrying out key aspects of the accords, especially in Hebron, for months. Palestinians fear that Netanyahu, regardless of his rhetoric, will insist on renegotiating what was a very specific hard-won deal.
Netanyahu said after talks with Christopher: "We did not propose opening the agreement. We suggested that within the confines of the existing agreement adjustments be made."
The Israeli leader has made clear his desire to modify security arrangements for Jewish settlers in Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns to be given self-rule.

In Gaza later with Arafat, Christopher said: "One of the things that has been clarified during my visit here is that the parties intend to negotiate within the four corners of the agreement...They do not seek to modify."
